name: The Five Vertebrate Classes
scope: The backbone family portrait: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals. Each rung sorts a harvested creature into its class by the one give-away trait (feathers = bird, fur + milk = mammal, scales + cold-blooded = reptile, wet skin + tadpole youth = amphibian, gills = fish). Top rung: birds ARE living theropod dinosaurs, so the 'five classes' hides a dinosaur among them.
source: Britannica; AMNH vertebrate overview
framing_note: Scene-led recognition: a kid names what they just skinned by its tell, not by memorizing a definition. Avoid 'What is a mammal?' shells; each rung leads with a concrete animal or trait. Keep taxonomy current (birds nested inside reptiles cladistically; note plainly at top tier without turning it into a lecture).

name: What Makes a Mammal
scope: The three hidden signatures every mammal shares: milk (mammary glands, the name-giving trait), hair/fur, and three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that no other animal has. Warm-blooded and mostly live-bearing. Payoff rung: those three ear bones started as reptile jaw bones.
source: Britannica; AMNH; UCMP Berkeley
framing_note: Scene-led: the surprise is the three-ear-bones signature (invisible from outside, unique to mammals). Concrete handle over jargon; keep the jaw-bone-to-ear-bone evolution factual and plain, no theology.

name: What Makes a Bird
scope: Feathers (the one trait no other living animal has), toothless beaks, hard-shelled eggs, warm blood, and air-filled hollow bones that make flight possible. Payoff: feathers evolved before flight, and birds descend from theropod dinosaurs.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; AMNH
framing_note: Feathers = the defining tell (leads every rung). Scene-led, not 'define bird.' Dinosaur ancestry stated as standard biology.

name: What Makes a Reptile / Amphibian (the wet-skin vs dry-scale split)
scope: Reptiles: dry keratin scales, shelled eggs laid on land, ectothermic. Amphibians: smooth permeable skin they breathe through, eggs in water, a larval water-phase (tadpole) before metamorphosis. The give-away: touch it — a snake is dry, a frog is wet.
source: Britannica; AmphibiaWeb; AMNH
framing_note: The dry-vs-wet skin contrast is the memorable handle. Scene-led. Distractors: confuse newt/salamander (amphibian) with lizard (reptile). No outdated 'cold-blooded' as the only frame — pair with ectotherm at T3.

name: The Three Kinds of Fish
scope: Bony fish (the vast majority — salmon, tuna, bass), cartilaginous fish (sharks and rays, skeletons of cartilage not bone), and jawless fish (lampreys and hagfish, mouths that are sucking discs, no jaw). Payoff: a shark has no single bone in its body.
source: Britannica; FishBase; AMNH
framing_note: Scene-led sorting of a caught fish. The shark-has-no-bones and lamprey-has-no-jaw facts are the wonder hooks. Distractors mix the three groups.

name: The Egg-Laying Mammals (Monotremes)
scope: Only five living species break the mammal rules: the platypus and four echidna species lay eggs yet still make milk. No nipples — milk oozes through patches of skin. The platypus also has a venomous spur and a duck bill that senses electricity.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; AMNH
framing_note: Wonder-led: the platypus is a rule-breaking mash-up (bill, spur, eggs, milk-through-skin). Real binomial Ornithorhynchus anatinus if named. Only 5 living monotreme species — state exactly. No anthropomorphizing.

name: The Pouch-Bearers (Marsupials)
scope: Kangaroo, koala, wombat, Tasmanian devil, opossum — mammals whose young are born as pink jellybean-sized embryos and crawl to a pouch to finish growing. The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial native to North America. A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a grape.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; AMNH
framing_note: The grape-sized newborn crawling to the pouch is the memorable image (also covers marsupial_pouch_development). Scene-led. Opossum-only-in-N-America is a good 'huh' rung.

name: Warm-Blooded vs Cold-Blooded, Done Right (endotherm vs ectotherm)
scope: The precise idea behind 'warm/cold blooded': endotherms burn food to heat themselves from inside (mammals, birds), ectotherms take their temperature from the environment (reptiles, most fish, amphibians) — which is why a lizard basks on a rock at dawn. Edge cases: tuna and some sharks keep parts of themselves warm.
source: Britannica; Khan Academy biology
framing_note: The basking-lizard scene makes the concept concrete rather than a definition. Teach the term before testing it. Regional endothermy in tuna is a genuine 'not so simple' payoff.

name: The Four Kinds of Arthropod
scope: The most successful body plan on Earth splits by leg count and habit: insects (6 legs, 3 body parts), arachnids (8 legs — spiders, scorpions, ticks), crustaceans (mostly aquatic — crabs, lobsters, shrimp), and myriapods (centipedes and millipedes, many legs). Count the legs to name the group.
source: Britannica; AMNH invertebrate zoology
framing_note: Leg-count as the sorting handle — a spider isn't an insect because it has 8 legs. Scene-led. Distractors put a spider in with insects, a centipede with crustaceans.

name: The Insect Orders (beetles rule the world)
scope: The big insect orders: Coleoptera (beetles — the largest order of animals on Earth, ~400,000 named species; 'God has an inordinate fondness for beetles'), Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths), Diptera (flies, one pair of wings), Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps). Payoff: roughly 1 in every 4 known animal species is a beetle.
source: Britannica; Smithsonian Entomology; Haldane beetle quote
framing_note: The staggering beetle count is the wonder payoff (number built up as a punchline, not a cold stat). The Haldane 'inordinate fondness for beetles' line is a dinner-table hook. Scene-led.

name: The Mollusk Classes (snail, clam, octopus — same phylum?!)
scope: One phylum stretches from a garden snail to a genius octopus: gastropods (snails, slugs — one muscular foot), bivalves (clams, oysters, mussels — two hinged shells, no head), and cephalopods (octopus, squid, cuttlefish, nautilus — 'head-foot,' arms around the mouth). The surprise: an oyster and an octopus are cousins.
source: Britannica; AMNH; MBARI
framing_note: The reveal that a clam and an octopus share a phylum is the hook. Scene-led. Sets up the octopus ladder. Distractors: put a starfish (echinoderm) or barnacle (crustacean) among mollusks.

name: The Octopus
scope: The keystone alien-on-Earth ladder: three hearts (two pump the gills, one the body; the body heart stops when it swims, so it prefers crawling); blue copper-based blood; a distributed 'nine brains' nervous system with two-thirds of neurons in the arms, so a severed arm can still grab; opens jars and hunts by touch; changes color with chromatophores/iridophores/leucophores while being colorblind (it may sense color through its skin); the coconut octopus carries shell halves as portable armor (first documented invertebrate tool use); the mimic octopus impersonates 15+ species.
source: Britannica; AMNH; MBARI; Godfrey-Smith 'Other Minds'; Finn et al. 2009 (coconut octopus)
framing_note: The bank's marquee wonder ladder — one deep story, one fact per rung, T2 (three hearts) climbing to T5 (colorblind-yet-camouflaging paradox, skin-based light sensing which is research-in-progress). No anthropomorphizing intelligence as human thought; describe behaviors (solves, opens, mimics). Real binomials only. Absorbs cephalopod_intelligence, tool_use_octopus, octopus_camouflage.

name: Jellyfish, Coral, and Anemones (Cnidarians)
scope: The stinging-cell phylum: jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydra, built on radial symmetry with no brain and no bones. Their weapon is the nematocyst — a microscopic harpoon that fires in under a millisecond, one of the fastest movements in all of biology. A coral reef is millions of tiny animals building limestone cities.
source: Britannica; AMNH; NOAA coral reef resources
framing_note: The harpoon-firing nematocyst is the vivid adaptation payoff. Scene-led (a swimmer brushes a tentacle). No 'define cnidarian.' Coral-as-colony-of-animals is a strong reveal rung.

name: Sea Stars and the Five-Fold Body (Echinoderms)
scope: Sea stars, sea urchins, sand dollars, sea cucumbers — spiny-skinned animals with five-fold radial symmetry and a water-powered hydraulic system of tube feet. A sea star can push its own stomach out of its body to digest a clam, and many can regrow a whole body from a single arm.
source: Britannica; AMNH; MBARI
framing_note: The stomach-eversion feeding and arm-regeneration are the retell-at-dinner payoffs. Scene-led. Avoid 'starfish' as the class name in the answer where 'sea star' is the accurate term; distractors can use the misnomer.

name: The Segmented Worms (Annelids)
scope: Earthworms, leeches, and bristly marine polychaetes — worms built from repeated segments like a stack of rings. The earthworm eats its way through soil and is farmed by every gardener; the medicinal leech was standard medical equipment for centuries and is still FDA-cleared for reattaching severed fingers.
source: Britannica; AMNH
framing_note: The leech-still-used-in-modern-surgery fact is the surprise payoff. Scene-led. Keep segmentation concrete (a stack of rings). No medical advice framing.

name: How Many Animals Are There? (species counts)
scope: Scientists estimate roughly 8.7 million animal species exist, but only about 1.4 million have been named and described — most of life is still unknown. Insects make up around three-quarters of all described animals; beetles alone outnumber every mammal, bird, reptile, and amphibian combined.
source: Mora et al. 2011 (PLoS Biology, ~8.7M estimate); IUCN; Britannica
framing_note: Numbers here only work because the stem builds the 'most of life is undiscovered' wonder first (payoff, not cold stat). Scene-led framing: a scientist naming a new beetle. The insect-dominance fact lands the scale.

name: Egg-Layers vs Live-Bearers (and eggs that hatch inside)
scope: The basic split: oviparous animals lay eggs (birds, most fish, reptiles), viviparous animals give live birth (most mammals). The twist: ovoviviparous animals like some sharks and snakes grow eggs that hatch inside the mother, so she appears to give live birth without a placenta.
source: Britannica; AMNH
framing_note: The ovoviviparous 'eggs that hatch inside' twist is the memorable rung. Teach the plain distinction first at T2, then the surprise at T3. Scene-led. Distractors swap the three modes.

name: Virgin Birth in Animals (parthenogenesis)
scope: Some animals reproduce with no father at all: whiptail lizards are all-female species, a bonnethead shark gave virgin birth in a US aquarium, and a captive Komodo dragon at Chester Zoo laid fertile eggs while never having met a male. The offspring are made from the mother alone.
source: Britannica; Nature (Komodo parthenogenesis, Watts et al. 2006); Chapman et al. 2007 (bonnethead)
framing_note: The captive-Komodo virgin-birth mystery is the hook (the zoo was baffled). Scene-led. State factually, no sensationalizing beyond the documented cases; real species only.

name: Animals That Change Sex (sequential hermaphrodites)
scope: Clownfish live in a strict hierarchy: all are born male, and when the dominant female dies the biggest male turns into the new female (so in Finding Nemo, Nemo's dad would have become his mom). Many wrasses do the reverse — the dominant female becomes male. Sex is a role that can flip.
source: Britannica; reef-fish biology literature
framing_note: The Finding Nemo clownfish twist is the ultimate dinner-table retell. Scene-led. Present as observed reef biology, plainly, without projecting onto human debates (this is fish life-history, stays neutral biology).

name: Many Cheap Young vs Few Pampered Ones (r vs K selection)
scope: Two strategies for making a future: a codfish releases millions of eggs and abandons them all, betting a few survive (r-selected); an elephant has one calf every several years and guards it for a decade (K-selected). Ocean sunfish lay the record ~300 million eggs at once.
source: Britannica; MacArthur & Wilson island biogeography; ocean sunfish fecundity records
framing_note: The cod-vs-elephant contrast makes the abstract trade-off concrete before naming it. Teach r/K after the scene. The sunfish 300-million-egg number is a built-up payoff.

name: Peacocks, Antlers, and the Cost of Beauty (sexual selection)
scope: Darwin's second big idea: traits that make survival harder can win because they win mates. A peacock's train is heavy and dangerous but females choose the showiest; a stag's antlers are grown and dropped every year for combat; birds-of-paradise clear a stage and dance. The handicap is the point.
source: Darwin 'The Descent of Man' 1871; Britannica; Cornell Lab (birds-of-paradise)
framing_note: The 'beauty that costs' paradox is the hook. Scene-led (a peahen choosing). Standard evolutionary biology — attribute to Darwin as context, not an 'X said Y' stem. No anthropomorphizing of choice.

name: Seeing With Sound (echolocation)
scope: Bats and dolphins map the dark by shouting and listening to the echoes — a bat can pinpoint a mosquito in total blackness, a dolphin can 'see' a fish buried in sand. The bat screams so loudly it must briefly deafen its own ears to avoid harming itself between calls.
source: Britannica; Donald Griffin (coined 'echolocation'); AMNH
framing_note: The bat-must-deafen-itself and dolphin-sees-through-sand facts are the payoffs. Scene-led (hunting in total dark). Distractors: attribute echolocation to owls (they use hearing but not echolocation).

name: Sensing Electricity (electroreception)
scope: Some animals feel the electric fields living bodies give off. A shark's snout is dotted with jelly-filled pores (the ampullae of Lorenzini) that detect the heartbeat of a fish hiding under sand; the platypus hunts with its eyes, ears, and nose shut, steering entirely by the electric bill.
source: Britannica; AMNH; shark sensory biology literature
framing_note: The shark-detecting-a-hidden-heartbeat and eyes-shut-platypus facts are the wonder hooks. Concrete handle ('jelly-filled pores') over 'ampullae of Lorenzini' jargon in the stem; name can be the answer or context. Scene-led.

name: The Bird That Reads Earth's Magnetism (magnetoreception)
scope: Migrating birds fly thousands of miles to the same tree using Earth's magnetic field as a compass. The leading idea is that a light-sensitive protein (cryptochrome) in the retina may let a robin literally see the field as a pattern of light — a mechanism still being worked out.
source: Britannica; Mouritsen & Ritz cryptochrome research; recent European robin studies
framing_note: The 'bird may SEE the magnetic field' image is the hook. Flag honestly that the cryptochrome mechanism is research-in-progress, not settled. Scene-led (a robin navigating). No overstating certainty.

name: A Dog's Nose (dog olfaction)
scope: A dog smells a world we can't imagine: roughly 300 million scent receptors to a human's 6 million, and a slice of brain devoted to smell about 40 times larger relatively. A trained dog can detect a teaspoon of sugar diluted in two Olympic swimming pools, and reads time by how a scent has faded.
source: Britannica; Alexandra Horowitz 'Being a Dog'; canine olfaction literature
framing_note: The scale comparisons (two swimming pools; smelling the passage of time) are the payoffs — number as constructed punchline, not cold stat. Scene-led. Ties forward to Pillar 3 detection dogs but stays about the biology here.

name: Seeing Colors We Can't (bird UV vision)
scope: Many birds see ultraviolet light, opening a hidden layer of the world: flowers wear UV runway-stripes pointing to nectar, some berries glow, and birds that look identical to us (like male and female blue tits) are obviously different in UV. A kestrel can even follow the UV-glowing urine trails of voles.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; kestrel UV vole-trail studies
framing_note: The kestrel-follows-glowing-pee-trails fact is the retell payoff. Scene-led. Present the invisible-to-us UV world concretely.

name: The Snake That Sees Heat (pit vipers)
scope: Rattlesnakes, pythons, and other pit vipers have heat-sensing pits between eye and nostril that build an infrared image of warm prey — a snake can strike a mouse in absolute darkness by its body heat alone, effectively seeing a thermal picture layered over its normal vision.
source: Britannica; herpetology sensory literature; TRPA1 heat-channel research
framing_note: The 'strikes in total darkness by heat' scene is the hook. Concrete handle ('heat-sensing pits') beats 'facial pit organ' jargon in the stem. Scene-led.

name: The Mantis Shrimp's Eyes
scope: The mantis shrimp has 16 types of color receptor to a human's 3, plus the ability to see polarized and circular-polarized light — the only animals known to do so. But the twist (2014, Thoen & Marshall) is that they're actually POOR at telling similar colors apart: instead of comparing signals like us, they seem to use a fast scanning recognition system that's still being studied.
source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014 (Science, 'A Different Form of Color Vision'); Cronin/Marshall stomatopod reviews
framing_note: MANDATORY accuracy caution: do NOT claim mantis shrimp 'see more colors' as fact — the research overturned that. The genuine wonder is the paradox (16 receptors yet poor discrimination; a recognition-not-comparison system that is research-in-progress). Frame the correction itself as the payoff. Scene-led.

name: The Elephant's Rumble You Can't Hear (infrasound)
scope: Elephants talk in deep infrasound below human hearing (under 20 Hz) that rolls for miles across the savanna, and they pick up these calls partly through the ground — feeling a distant herd through the soles of their feet and their trunk pressed to the earth.
source: Katy Payne (elephant infrasound discovery); Caitlin O'Connell (seismic communication); Britannica
framing_note: The 'listening through their feet' image is the hook. Scene-led (herds coordinating across miles). No anthropomorphizing the calls into human language. Katy Payne as context, not an 'X said Y' stem.

name: How a Whale Hears (jaw as ear)
scope: Whales and dolphins hear through their jaws: a fat-filled channel in the lower jawbone catches underwater sound and pipes it straight to the inner ear, since ordinary outer ears would be useless in the deep. Sound travels roughly four to five times faster in water than in air.
source: Britannica; cetacean acoustics literature (Nummela et al. on jaw hearing)
framing_note: The 'hears through its jaw' fact is the surprise. Scene-led. Ties to whale evolution (Pillar 2) but stays about the living animal's sense here.

name: The Electric Eel
scope: Not a true eel but a South American knifefish that turns its body into a living battery: thousands of stacked electric cells fire together for a jolt up to 860 volts (the record, measured in Electrophorus voltai, one of three species named only in 2019 — named for Alessandro Volta, whose battery it inspired). It stuns prey, can leap to press its shock onto a threat, and navigates with weak electric pulses.
source: de Santana et al. 2019 (electric eel = 3 species; E. voltai 860V, Nature Communications); Kenneth Catania (leaping-attack studies)
framing_note: The 860V record and the Volta-battery naming are the payoffs (number built up as punchline). Accuracy: it's a knifefish, NOT a true eel; 860V belongs to E. voltai specifically; the 3-species split dates to 2019. Real binomials only. Absorbs electric_eel_voltage + electric_eel_shock.

name: The Tardigrade (water bear)
scope: A half-millimeter eight-legged 'water bear' that is nearly indestructible: by curling into a dried-out 'tun' (cryptobiosis) it survives boiling, freezing near absolute zero, crushing pressure, blasts of radiation, and even the raw vacuum of open space — tardigrades were exposed to space on a 2007 orbital mission and lived.
source: Britannica; Jönsson et al. 2008 (TARDIS space-exposure experiment); AMNH
framing_note: The 'survived open space' fact is the marquee payoff; each rung stacks one extreme it survives. Scene-led. Keep 'nearly indestructible' honest (they die eventually; cryptobiosis is the mechanism). Real, wondrous, factual.

name: The Axolotl
scope: A Mexican salamander that never grows up — it keeps its feathery gills and stays aquatic for life (neoteny) instead of turning into a land salamander. Its superpower is regeneration: it regrows whole limbs, parts of its heart, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord, scar-free. Nearly extinct in the wild (Lake Xochimilco) yet common in labs and aquariums.
source: Britannica; AMNH; regeneration research (e.g. Tanaka lab); IUCN (wild status)
framing_note: The regrows-its-own-brain fact is the payoff; neoteny (a 'Peter Pan' salamander) is the concrete handle. Scene-led. Note the wild-vs-lab paradox honestly. Real species Ambystoma mexicanum if named.

name: The Immortal Jellyfish
scope: Turritopsis dohrnii, a jellyfish the size of a pinky nail, can cheat death: when injured, starving, or old, its adult body reverts all the way back to its juvenile polyp stage and starts life over — like a butterfly turning back into a caterpillar. In principle this cycle can repeat forever, so it's called 'biologically immortal' (though predators and disease still kill it).
source: Britannica; Piraino et al. 1996 (transdifferentiation); Smithsonian Ocean
framing_note: The butterfly-back-to-caterpillar handle makes 'transdifferentiation' concrete. Accuracy: 'immortal' means it can escape aging, NOT that it can't be killed — state the caveat. Real binomial Turritopsis dohrnii. Scene-led.

name: The Mantis Shrimp's Punch
scope: The smasher mantis shrimp throws the fastest punch in the sea: its spring-loaded club accelerates like a .22 bullet, striking so fast it boils the water into imploding cavitation bubbles that flash with light and heat — a second shockwave that hits even if the first strike misses. It can crack aquarium glass and shatter crab shells.
source: Sheila Patek (mantis shrimp strike biomechanics, Nature 2004); Britannica
framing_note: The bullet-fast, water-boiling, twice-hitting punch is pure dinner-table wonder — build the cavitation as a payoff. Scene-led (cracking aquarium glass). Pair with the separate eyes ladder but keep this one about the strike. Factual biomechanics.

name: The Pistol Shrimp's Snap
scope: A shrimp barely 2 inches long snaps its oversized claw so fast it fires a bubble bullet — a collapsing cavitation bubble that momentarily reaches roughly 4,700°C (nearly the surface temperature of the sun) and stuns prey with the shockwave, not the claw itself. Colonies snapping together are loud enough to disrupt sonar.
source: Versluis et al. 2000 (snapping shrimp cavitation & sonoluminescence, Science); Britannica
framing_note: The 'as hot as the sun's surface for an instant' comparison is the payoff (number constructed as punchline). Accuracy: the heat is brief and localized in the collapsing bubble. Scene-led. Distinct from mantis shrimp (different animal, different mechanism).

name: The Mimic Octopus
scope: Thaumoctopus mimicus, discovered off Indonesia in 1998, is the impressionist of the sea: it doesn't just change color, it reshapes its body and movement to impersonate other animals — flattening and rippling like a venomous flatfish, trailing arms to become a banded sea snake, spreading out as a spiny lionfish — choosing the disguise that best scares off whatever is threatening it.
source: Norman, Finn & Tregenza 2001 (mimic octopus, Proc. Royal Society); Britannica
framing_note: The 'picks a costume to match the threat' behavior is the payoff. Real binomial, discovered 1998. Describe the imitation as observed behavior, not conscious intent (no anthropomorphizing). Scene-led. Cross-refs the octopus ladder but stands alone.

name: The Glass Frog
scope: A Central/South American frog with skin so transparent you can watch its heart beat through its belly. In 2022 scientists solved how it vanishes: while sleeping it pulls nearly 90% of its red blood cells out of circulation and packs them into a mirror-lined liver, turning see-through — then somehow avoids the deadly clots that would kill other animals.
source: Taboada, Delia et al. 2022 (Science; AMNH & Duke, photoacoustic imaging)
framing_note: The see-its-heartbeat and hides-its-own-blood facts are the payoffs. Recent (2022) research; state the RBC-in-liver mechanism accurately. Family Centrolenidae as context, concrete handle in stem. Scene-led. Genuinely research-fresh — cite the year.

name: The Naked Mole-Rat
scope: A wrinkled, nearly hairless, buck-toothed rodent that breaks the rules of mammal life: it lives in an insect-like colony ruled by a single breeding queen (eusocial, like ants), survives ~30 years when a mouse gets ~3, almost never gets cancer, feels no pain from acid or chili burns, and can go minutes with almost no oxygen by burning fructose like a plant.
source: Britannica; Buffenstein lab (longevity/cancer resistance); Park et al. 2017 (fructose metabolism, Science)
framing_note: A keystone weird-mammal ladder — each rung is one rule it breaks (queen, 30-year lifespan, cancer resistance, pain insensitivity, oxygen-free survival). Scene-led. All facts documented; no exaggeration ('almost never' not 'never' for cancer). Real, wondrous, factual.

name: The Hagfish's Slime
scope: A jawless, eel-shaped fish that defends itself by instantly gushing slime: a few grams of gland goo mixed with seawater expands into liters — enough to fill a bucket in seconds — clogging a predator's gills and mouth. To escape its own trap the hagfish ties itself into a knot and slides the knot down its body to wipe clean.
source: Britannica; Fudge lab (hagfish slime biomechanics); Vancouver Aquarium
framing_note: The bucket-of-slime-in-seconds and ties-itself-in-a-knot facts are the payoffs. Scene-led (a shark gagging on slime). Accuracy: hagfish is a jawless fish. Real and factual, no exaggeration beyond documented slime expansion.

name: The Peacock Spider
scope: A jumping spider from Australia the size of a grain of rice (about 5 mm) whose males lift a fan of electric-blue-and-red iridescent scales like a peacock and perform a leg-waving dance to court a female — who eats him if the show fails. The Maratus genus has dozens of species named partly by amateur naturalists photographing them.
source: Jürgen Otto (peacock spider documentation); Australian Museum; Maratus taxonomy literature
framing_note: The tiny-flamboyant-dancer image (and the fatal stakes) is the payoff. Scene-led. Genus Maratus as context. No anthropomorphizing the dance into intent beyond documented courtship behavior.

name: The Blue Whale (the largest ever)
scope: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived — bigger than any dinosaur — reaching about 30 m and up to ~200 tonnes. Its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant, its heart is the size of a small car, and a newborn calf gains around 90 kg (200 lb) a day on its mother's milk.
source: Britannica; NOAA Fisheries; AMNH
framing_note: T1 anchor (largest animal alive today / ever) climbing to vivid comparisons (tongue = an elephant; heart = a car; calf gains 200 lb/day). Numbers work as built-up payoffs. Scene-led. 'Bigger than any dinosaur' is accurate and a strong hook.

name: The Smallest Warm-Bloods (Etruscan shrew & bee hummingbird)
scope: At the tiny extreme of warm-blooded life: the Etruscan shrew is the smallest mammal by mass (~1.8 g, lighter than a coin) with a heart hammering around 1,500 beats a minute; the bee hummingbird of Cuba is the smallest bird (~5–6 cm, ~2 g) and beats its wings ~80 times a second. Both must eat almost constantly or starve within hours.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab (bee hummingbird); shrew physiology literature
framing_note: The 'must eat constantly or die by nightfall' fact frames the numbers as payoffs, not cold stats. Contrast pairs nicely with the blue whale. Scene-led. Absorbs etruscan_shrew_smallest + bee_hummingbird.

name: The Colossal Squid's Eyes
scope: The colossal squid (Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni) of the deep Antarctic has the largest eyes of any known animal — about the size of a basketball (~27 cm) — probably to catch the faint glow that warns of an approaching sperm whale, its main predator, in the black deep sea. Its arms bear swiveling hooks, not just suckers.
source: Britannica; Te Papa (specimen studies); Nilsson et al. 2012 (giant eyes & whale detection)
framing_note: The basketball-sized-eye-to-spot-a-whale hypothesis is the payoff. Real binomial Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni; distinguish from the giant squid (Architeuthis, different animal). Scene-led. Whale-detection function is well-supported but frame as the leading explanation.

name: The Lyrebird's Impressions
scope: Australia's superb lyrebird is the world's greatest vocal mimic: males weave into their courtship song flawless copies of other birds, and famously the human-made sounds of their habitat — camera shutters, car alarms, and even chainsaws — with an accuracy that can fool the animals and machines being imitated.
source: Britannica; David Attenborough / BBC lyrebird footage; Australian Museum
framing_note: The chainsaw-and-camera-shutter mimicry is the retell payoff. Scene-led. Note some famous captive imitations (chainsaws) are debated as to how common they are in the wild — keep to well-documented mimicry, don't overclaim.

name: The Archerfish's Aim
scope: The archerfish hunts by spitting: it fires a precise jet of water from below the surface to knock insects off overhanging leaves, and — remarkably — its brain corrects for the way light bends at the water's surface (refraction), so it aims at where the bug really is, not where it appears to be. It can learn to hit moving targets.
source: Britannica; Schuster et al. (archerfish shooting & learning studies)
framing_note: The 'does physics to correct for refraction' angle is the payoff. Scene-led (a bug knocked into the water). Present the aiming as observed skill, factual. No anthropomorphizing beyond documented learning behavior.

name: The Monarch Butterfly's Migration
scope: Every autumn monarchs stream up to 3,000 miles from Canada and the US to a few mountain forests in Mexico — but no single butterfly makes the round trip. It takes three to four generations to return north, so the butterflies arriving at the exact same overwintering trees have never been there, navigating by an inherited sun-compass.
source: Britannica; Monarch Watch; Reppert lab (sun-compass navigation)
framing_note: The 'great-great-grandchildren return to a place they've never seen' paradox is the hook. Scene-led. State the multi-generational fact accurately. Cross-refs monarch toxicity (defense ladder) but stays about migration here.

name: The Arctic Tern's Pole-to-Pole Flight
scope: The arctic tern makes the longest migration on Earth, flying from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic waters and back — a zig-zagging route totaling roughly 44,000 miles (70,000 km) a year. Because it chases endless summer at both poles, this small seabird sees more daylight than any other animal, and over a lifetime flies the distance of several trips to the Moon.
source: Egevang et al. 2010 (geolocator tracking, PNAS); Britannica
framing_note: The 'sees more sunlight than any animal' and 'lifetime = trips to the Moon' comparisons are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers built up, not cold. Longest-migration is well established.

name: The Salmon's Journey Home
scope: A salmon hatched in a tiny mountain stream swims to the open ocean for years, then finds its way back to the exact same stream to spawn — steering by Earth's magnetic field over the long haul and by the remembered smell of its home water for the final approach. Pacific species spawn once, then die, feeding the whole forest.
source: Britannica; Lohmann (magnetic imprinting); Hasler & Scholz (olfactory homing)
framing_note: The 'smells its way back to its birth stream' fact plus the spawn-then-die twist are the payoffs. Scene-led. State magnetic + olfactory navigation accurately. Ties to husbandry/aquaculture elsewhere but stays wild-behavior here.

name: The Dance Floor of Male Display (lekking)
scope: At a lek, males gather on a communal display ground and compete for watching females: sage grouse inflate booming air sacs on their chests, manakins moonwalk and snap their wings like firecrackers, and New Zealand's flightless kakapo booms from a bowl it digs to amplify the sound. Females wander through and pick the best performer.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab (manakin displays, sage grouse); kakapo recovery program
framing_note: The concrete displays (moonwalking manakin, booming kakapo bowl) make 'lek' memorable — teach the term after the scene. Scene-led. Documented behaviors only.

name: Colonies That Act Like One Animal (eusociality)
scope: In a few animals, most individuals give up breeding to serve one queen and raise her young — the whole colony works like a single body. Ants, honeybees, and termites do it, and so, uniquely among mammals, does the naked mole-rat. A single leafcutter-ant colony can farm fungus and number millions.
source: Britannica; E.O. Wilson 'The Insect Societies'; leafcutter ant biology
framing_note: The 'colony as one super-organism' idea and the mammal exception (naked mole-rat) are the hooks. Teach eusociality after the concrete example. Scene-led. Cross-refs the mole-rat ladder.

name: Crows That Make Tools
scope: New Caledonian crows don't just use sticks — they manufacture tools, snipping and shaping hooked twigs and barbed leaf-edges to fish grubs out of holes, and they pass techniques to their young. In lab tests one crow, Betty, bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a bucket, and crows solve multi-step puzzles like the fable of the crow and the pitcher.
source: Britannica; Alex Kacelnik / Oxford (Betty the crow); Gavin Hunt (tool manufacture)
framing_note: The 'bent a wire into a hook, unprompted' and 'passes Aesop's pitcher test' facts are payoffs. Scene-led. Present as documented problem-solving, not human-level thought. Cross-refs crow_intelligence in the cognition strand; keep this about tool-making.

name: The Bee's Waggle Dance
scope: A returning honeybee tells the hive where to find flowers by dancing: it waggles in a straight line whose ANGLE (relative to straight up) encodes the direction toward the sun, and whose DURATION encodes the distance. Karl von Frisch cracked this code and won a Nobel Prize — a language of movement, in the dark, on a vertical comb.
source: Karl von Frisch (waggle dance decoding, 1973 Nobel); Britannica
framing_note: The 'a dance that gives GPS coordinates' reveal is the payoff. Scene-led. von Frisch as context (Nobel), not an 'X said Y' stem. State angle=direction, duration=distance accurately.

name: The Mirror Test (self-recognition)
scope: Put a mark on an animal and show it a mirror: if it touches the mark on its OWN body, it seems to recognize itself. A short, surprising club has passed — great apes, dolphins, elephants (one touched a painted X on its head), and Eurasian magpies among birds — while most animals treat the mirror as a stranger. A recent cleaner-wrasse fish result has scientists arguing about the test itself.
source: Gordon Gallup (mark test, 1970); Reiss & Marino (dolphins); Plotnik/de Waal (elephants); Prior et al. (magpies)
framing_note: The specific passers (an elephant touching a mark on its head; a magpie) are the payoffs. Scene-led. Present as a debated-but-real measure; flag the cleaner-wrasse controversy honestly (what the test proves is contested). No overclaiming animal 'self-awareness' as settled.

name: Alex the African Grey Parrot
scope: Over 30 years with scientist Irene Pepperberg, an African grey parrot named Alex learned to use about 100 words meaningfully — naming colors and shapes, counting to six, grasping 'same' and 'different,' and even asking what color HE was. His reported last words to Pepperberg the night before he died in 2007 were 'You be good, I love you.'
source: Irene Pepperberg 'The Alex Studies' / 'Alex & Me'; peer-reviewed avian cognition papers
framing_note: The 'asked what color he was' and the last-words fact are the payoffs. Scene-led. Present Alex's abilities as documented and Pepperberg's careful claims — avoid overselling parrot 'understanding' beyond the research. Pepperberg as context.

name: The Signing Apes (Koko & Washoe)
scope: In the 20th century researchers raised apes with sign language: Washoe the chimpanzee (Gardners, from the 1960s) learned ~350 signs and was the first non-human to acquire a human language element; Koko the gorilla (Francine Patterson) reportedly used ~1,000 signs and famously mourned her kitten. How much real grammar the apes grasped is genuinely debated among scientists.
source: Gardner & Gardner (Washoe); Francine Patterson (Koko); Herbert Terrace (Nim / the skeptical case)
framing_note: The vivid moments (Koko and her kitten) are the hooks. MANDATORY balance: state plainly that the extent of real language/grammar is contested (cite the skeptical side, e.g. Terrace's Nim critique) — do NOT present ape 'language' as settled. Scene-led. Absorbs koko_gorilla + washoe_chimp.

name: Dolphins With a Culture (sponging)
scope: In Shark Bay, Australia, some bottlenose dolphins wear sea sponges on their beaks like gloves to protect them while rooting for fish on the rough seabed — and this trick is taught by mothers to their daughters down the generations, a genuine learned tradition (culture) passed on rather than instinct.
source: Krützen et al. 2005 (sponging as cultural transmission, PNAS); Shark Bay Dolphin Research
framing_note: The 'wears a sponge as a tool, taught mother-to-daughter' fact is the payoff and the definition of animal culture. Scene-led. Present transmission as documented. No anthropomorphizing.

name: Elephants and Their Dead
scope: Elephants react to death unlike almost any other animal: herds have been documented stopping to investigate the bones and tusks of dead elephants — touching and turning them gently with trunks and feet, and lingering — grief-like behavior that researchers study carefully without claiming to know the animal's inner experience.
source: Britannica; Cynthia Moss / Amboseli Elephant Research; McComb et al. (responses to remains)
framing_note: MANDATORY caution: describe 'grief-LIKE behavior' and 'documented investigation of remains' — do NOT state 'the elephant mourned/cried' as fact (the doc's headline anti-pattern). The restraint IS the honest wonder. Scene-led.

name: The Skunk's Spray
scope: A skunk's warning is real: it aims a spray of sulfur compounds (thiols) from glands under its tail that can hit a target several feet away and be smelled up to a mile off, clinging for days. It gives fair warning first — stamping, hissing, raising its tail — and can even do a handstand (the spotted skunk) before firing.
source: Britannica; skunk chemistry (thiols); spotted skunk handstand behavior
framing_note: The handstand-before-spraying and smellable-a-mile-off facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Concrete handle ('sulfur compounds / thiols') over pure chemistry jargon. Factual.

name: Playing Dead (opossum thanatosis)
scope: When a threat is overwhelming, the Virginia opossum doesn't decide to fake death — it involuntarily flops into a comatose state, tongue out, eyes glazed, and oozes a foul green corpse-smelling fluid from glands, becoming so convincingly 'dead' that a predator loses interest. It can stay this way for minutes to hours before snapping out of it.
source: Britannica; thanatosis (tonic immobility) literature
framing_note: The 'it's INVOLUNTARY, not acting' twist plus the corpse-smell detail are the payoffs. Scene-led ('playing possum' is the folk name, thanatosis the term). State it's a reflex, not a choice — accuracy matters here.

name: The Pufferfish's Poison
scope: A pufferfish carries tetrodotoxin, a neurotoxin roughly 1,000 times deadlier than cyanide, with no antidote — it paralyzes the muscles while the victim stays conscious. In Japan it's the delicacy fugu, which by law only licensed chefs trained for years may prepare, cutting away the toxic organs; a wrong cut can kill the diner.
source: Britannica; tetrodotoxin toxicology; Japanese fugu licensing
framing_note: The 'more deadly than cyanide, no antidote, and people pay to eat it' tension is the payoff. Scene-led (the licensed fugu chef). Accuracy: puffers acquire TTX via diet/bacteria; state deadliness without recipe detail. Cross-refs cooking bank but the animal biology stays here.

name: The Monarch's Poisonous Childhood
scope: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed — a plant toxic to most animals — and instead of being harmed they store the poison (cardenolides) in their bodies, staying toxic as adult butterflies. Their bright orange-and-black is a billboard warning, and the harmless viceroy butterfly copies the pattern to freeload on the monarch's bad reputation.
source: Britannica; monarch cardenolide sequestration; Batesian/Müllerian mimicry (viceroy)
framing_note: The 'eats poison to become poison, and a copycat exploits it' story is the payoff (and teaches warning coloration + mimicry). Scene-led. Note the viceroy is now considered co-mimic (Müllerian), not purely a harmless fake — keep it accurate.

name: The Bombardier Beetle's Chemical Cannon
scope: The bombardier beetle mixes chemical weapons on demand: it stores hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide separately, then combines them in a reaction chamber where enzymes trigger a boiling explosion that blasts out the tail end as a pulsing spray near 100°C (the boiling point of water) — aimed with a swiveling nozzle straight at an attacker's face.
source: Britannica; Eisner & Aneshansley (bombardier beetle spray mechanism, pulsed jet studies)
framing_note: The 'mixes two chemicals to fire a boiling spray from a swiveling nozzle' fact is the payoff. Scene-led. The pulsed-jet, near-100°C mechanism is well studied — state accurately. Concrete over jargon.

name: The Chameleon
scope: Two superpowers in one lizard: eyes that swivel independently so it watches two directions at once, then lock together to judge distance before a strike; and a tongue that launches faster than a sports car accelerates, longer than its own body, to snatch an insect. Its color change is more about mood, temperature, and signalling than blending in.
source: Britannica; Milinkovitch 2015 (chameleon color-change nanocrystals, Nature Communications)
framing_note: The independent-swiveling-eyes and faster-than-a-car tongue are the payoffs. Accuracy: correct the myth - color change is mainly signalling/thermoregulation, NOT primarily camouflage (recent nanocrystal research). Scene-led.

name: The Cuttlefish's Skin
scope: A cephalopod that runs hypnotic color waves down its body to stun prey and can split its display in half - courting a female on one flank while flashing a male-repelling pattern on the other. Like the octopus it is colorblind, yet it is a master of color, and it also controls the 3D texture of its skin to match rock or coral.
source: Britannica; Marine Biological Laboratory (cuttlefish camouflage); Hanlon cephalopod research
framing_note: The two-messages-at-once and colorblind-master-of-color paradox are the payoffs. Real animal, factual. Scene-led. Pairs with the octopus ladder but distinct.

name: The Star-Nosed Mole
scope: A blind mole with a nose ringed by 22 pink tentacles - the fastest-eating mammal known, identifying and swallowing prey in about a quarter of a second. The star is not for smelling: it is a touch organ packed with more than 100,000 nerve fibers that maps the world faster than the eye reads a page.
source: Kenneth Catania (star-nosed mole research, Vanderbilt); Britannica
framing_note: The eats-in-a-quarter-second and sees-with-its-nose facts are the payoffs (numbers built as punchlines). Real species Condylura cristata. Scene-led. Accuracy: the star is a touch organ, not for smell.

name: The Firefly's Cold Light (bioluminescence)
scope: A firefly makes cold light - nearly all of the energy becomes glow, not heat, from a reaction of luciferin, luciferase, and oxygen. Each species flashes its own Morse-code pattern to find a mate; the femme-fatale Photuris female mimics another species' flash code to lure and eat the males who answer.
source: Britannica; Photuris predatory mimicry literature (Lloyd); bioluminescence chemistry
framing_note: The near-perfect-efficiency cold light and the femme-fatale-firefly hunt are the payoffs. Scene-led. Real genera. Factual chemistry (luciferin/luciferase) as concrete handle.

name: The Anglerfish of the Deep
scope: A deep-sea predator that dangles a glowing lure (lit by symbiotic bacteria) in front of its fanged mouth to draw prey through the black. The stranger fact: the tiny male is a fraction of the female's size and, in some species, bites onto her and permanently fuses to her body, becoming a living sperm sac sharing her bloodstream.
source: Britannica; Ceratioid anglerfish reproduction (Pietsch); deep-sea biology
framing_note: The glowing-lure hunt and the fused-parasitic-male fact are the payoffs (the male fact is genuinely astonishing). Scene-led. State the sexual parasitism factually, real ceratioid biology. No sensationalizing beyond the documented.

name: The Honey Badger's Nerve
scope: A small mustelid famous for fearlessness: loose, thick, rubbery skin lets it twist around and bite back even when a predator has it in its jaws; it shrugs off bee stings to raid hives and has notable resistance to snake venom, recovering after cobra bites that would kill most animals its size.
source: Britannica; honey badger (Mellivora capensis) natural history; venom-resistance observations
framing_note: The loose-skin-lets-it-turn-in-a-predators-mouth and venom-resistance facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Real species Mellivora capensis. Keep 'fearless' concrete via the adaptations, no meme-tone.

name: The Sloth's Slow Life
scope: The sloth is built for near-zero effort: it digests a leaf over about a month, moves so slowly that green algae grows in its fur (camouflage plus a private garden), and climbs down its tree only about once a week to relieve itself. Hanging upside down, its hair parts the wrong way so rain runs off.
source: Britannica; sloth physiology; sloth-algae-moth symbiosis research
framing_note: The month-long digestion, algae-in-the-fur garden, and weekly bathroom trip are the retell payoffs. Scene-led. Real biology, factual. No anthropomorphizing 'lazy' - it is an energy strategy.

name: The Woodpecker's Head
scope: A woodpecker hammers a tree up to 20 times a second, thousands of times a day, and does not concuss itself: it has a tongue that wraps up and around the back of the skull (anchoring near the nostril) which, with dense spongy bone and a tightly packed brain, helps manage the shock. Recent research argues the small head acts less like a shock absorber and more like a stiff hammer.
source: Britannica; van Wassenbergh 2022 (woodpecker head as stiff hammer, Current Biology)
framing_note: The tongue-wraps-around-the-skull fact is the payoff. Accuracy: note the 2022 correction - the head works more as a stiff hammer than a cushioned shock absorber (research updated the old story). Scene-led.

name: The Platypus, Head to Tail
scope: Beyond laying eggs, the platypus is a walking checklist of oddities: a leathery duck bill that reads electric fields underwater, webbed feet, a beaver-like tail that stores fat, venomous ankle spurs on the males, and - under UV light - fur that glows biofluorescent green-blue, a trait discovered only in 2020.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; Anich et al. 2020 (platypus biofluorescence, Mammalia)
framing_note: A deeper companion to the monotreme ladder, focused on the platypus's stacked oddities (venom spur, electro-bill, 2020 glow-in-UV discovery). Real binomial Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Scene-led. Factual, no anthropomorphizing.

name: The Giraffe's Impossible Neck
scope: The tallest animal solves problems its height creates: a heart about 60 cm long pumps at roughly double human blood pressure to reach the brain two metres up, tight leg skin acts like a pilot's g-suit to stop blood pooling, and special valves keep it from blacking out when it swings its head down to drink. Its neck has just seven bones - the same number as a human.
source: Britannica; giraffe cardiovascular physiology literature
framing_note: The double-blood-pressure heart, the g-suit legs, and the same-seven-neck-bones-as-a-human facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers built as punchlines. Factual anatomy.

name: The Cheetah's Sprint
scope: The fastest land animal hits about 100 km/h (60+ mph) in a few strides, using a flexible spine that coils and uncoils like a spring so all four feet leave the ground twice per stride, semi-retractable claws for grip like running spikes, and a long tail as a rudder for hairpin turns - but it overheats fast and can only sprint for seconds.
source: Britannica; cheetah locomotion biomechanics (Wilson et al. 2013, Nature)
framing_note: The spine-as-spring, claws-as-spikes, tail-as-rudder mechanics and the overheating limit are the payoffs. Scene-led (a chase). Factual. Distractors: pronghorn (fastest over distance), peregrine (fastest in a dive).

name: The Peregrine Falcon's Dive
scope: The fastest animal on Earth is not a runner but a diver: a peregrine falcon in a hunting stoop exceeds 300 km/h (about 240 mph), fast enough that little cones of bone in its nostrils are thought to keep the rushing air from bursting its lungs, and a special third eyelid wipes the eye clear mid-dive.
source: Britannica; peregrine stoop aerodynamics; falcon nostril-cone hypothesis
framing_note: The 240-mph dive and the nostril-cones-so-its-lungs-don't-burst fact are the payoffs. Scene-led. Accuracy: 'fastest animal' = in a dive specifically; the nostril-cone role is a well-cited hypothesis - frame accordingly.

name: The Bombardier of the Sky: Dragonfly Flight
scope: A dragonfly is the deadliest hunter in the animal world by success rate, catching prey in roughly 95% of attempts - because it can beat its four wings independently, hover, fly backwards, and calculate an interception course to where the prey WILL be, not where it is. Its eyes wrap the head in nearly 30,000 lenses.
source: Britannica; dragonfly interception & predation-success research (Combes, Leonardo)
framing_note: The 95%-success 'best predator' stat and the calculates-an-interception fact are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers built up. Present as documented; independent four-wing flight is factual.

name: The Wood Frog That Freezes Solid
scope: The wood frog survives winter by freezing: up to two-thirds of its body water turns to ice, its heart stops, and it stops breathing - clinically dead for weeks or months. It floods its cells with glucose as antifreeze to protect them, then in spring it thaws, the heart restarts, and it hops away.
source: Britannica; wood frog (Rana sylvatica) freeze-tolerance research (Storey lab)
framing_note: The 'heart stops, it's basically dead, then it thaws and hops off' arc is the payoff. Scene-led. Real species Rana/Lithobates sylvatica. Factual cryoprotection (glucose antifreeze). No overstatement - it is genuine freeze tolerance.

name: The Sea Otter's Toolkit
scope: A sea otter carries a favourite rock in a pouch of loose skin under its arm and uses it as an anvil to smash open shellfish on its chest while floating - one of the few tool-using mammals. It has the densest fur of any animal (up to a million hairs per square inch) because, unlike other sea mammals, it has almost no blubber to keep warm.
source: Britannica; Monterey Bay Aquarium; sea otter tool-use & thermoregulation research
framing_note: The rock-anvil-in-an-armpit-pouch tool use and densest-fur-because-no-blubber facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Numbers (fur density) built as punchline. Factual.

name: The Coelacanth: A Fish From the Age of Dinosaurs
scope: In 1938 a museum curator, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, recognized an ugly blue fish in a South African trawler's catch as something thought extinct for 66 million years - a coelacanth, a lobe-finned fish close to the ancestors of land animals. It has fleshy limb-like fins, gives live birth, and a hinged skull found nowhere else alive today.
source: Britannica; coelacanth (Latimeria) discovery (Courtenay-Latimer, Smith 1939); Latimeria biology
framing_note: The 'a living fossil hauled up from a fishing boat by someone who recognized it' story is the payoff; the lobe fins connect to the tetrapod-origins theme (Pillar 2) but stays about the living animal. Scene-led. Real genus Latimeria. Factual - not literally unchanged, but a deep relict lineage.

name: The Horseshoe Crab's Blue Blood
scope: A helmet-shaped animal that has crawled the seas for over 400 million years - older than the dinosaurs, and more closely related to spiders than to crabs. Its blood is copper-blue and so sensitive to bacterial toxins that a clotting extract from it is used to test that vaccines and medical devices are safe, making it quietly vital to modern medicine.
source: Britannica; Limulus amebocyte lysate (LAL) test; horseshoe crab natural history
framing_note: The 400-million-year 'living fossil', spider-not-crab, and blue-blood-tests-your-vaccines facts are the payoffs. Scene-led. Real animal (Limulus). Factual. The medical use is genuine and a strong 'huh' rung.
